title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, USA
caption: Roaming the grasslands
subtitle: A bison in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, USA
description:
Bison are among the largest land mammals in the world, capable of weighing up to 900 kilograms and reaching speeds of 65 kilometres per hour despite their massive size. Despite often being called a buffalo, the American bison is not one of the true buffaloes, which are native to Africa and Asia. Its scientific name, Bison bison, leaves little room for confusion.
Its muscular shoulder hump helps it swing its head side to side, clearing snow to reach grass underneath. Both males and females grow horns and beards. Their tails offer clues about their mood: a swishing tail generally signals calm, while a raised tail may indicate agitation.

title: Lanterns for Diwali in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
caption: A celebration that shines
subtitle: Diwali (Festival of Lights)
description:
What happens when the darkest night of the year gets the brightest celebration? Diwali. The Festival of Lights is celebrated by millions worldwide, bringing together diyas, lanterns, rangoli, prayers, sweets and family gatherings.
The name Diwali comes from the Sanskrit 'dipavali', meaning 'row of lights'. The celebration falls on Amavasya, the new-moon night in the Hindu month of Kartik. Across India, the festival carries different stories and traditions. In North India, it marks Lord Rama's return to Ayodhya; in parts of South India and Nepal, it is linked to Lord Krishna's victory over Narakasura. In Bengal, the festival honours the goddess Kali. Jains and Sikhs also observe Diwali for important religious reasons.
Diwali is also widely celebrated across the UK, where generations of families and communities come together to mark the occasion. Celebrations range from gatherings at homes and places of worship to colourful public events, with lights, music, food and fireworks all part of the festivities.

title: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
caption: Where art finds its rhythm
subtitle: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
description:
Cross the Guadalquivir River in Seville, the capital of Spain's Andalusia region, and the city's rhythm seems to change. On the other side lies Triana, a colourful neighbourhood where ceramics, flamenco and local traditions are woven into everyday life. Since the 19th century, the Isabel II Bridge, also known as the Triana Bridge, has connected the neighbourhood to Seville's historic centre.
Step off the bridge and Triana's distinctive character comes into view. The neighbourhood has a long tradition of pottery and tilemaking, and colourful azulejos still brighten facades and workshops. Its streets have also played an important role in the history of flamenco, an art form deeply associated with Triana. Along Calle Betis, brightly painted buildings face the Guadalquivir.
Triana isn't defined by a single monument. Its appeal lies in its mix of artisans and markets, music and tiled courtyards, riverside terraces and narrow streets. Seville may be just across the water, but Triana has a spirit all its own.

title: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
caption: Licensed to chill
subtitle: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
description:
From above, Rose Island looks like a brushstroke of green surrounded by every shade of blue. Just five kilometres east of Paradise Island in The Bahamas, this slender cay trades busy roads and city blocks for sandy shores, shallow waters and an inland lagoon. Its peaceful appearance comes with a touch of movie drama. Rose Island was used as a filming location for the 1965 James Bond adventure Thunderball, including the explosive destruction of the Disco Volante.
Beyond its cinematic cameo, Rose Island offers a glimpse of what makes The Bahamas so striking. The island is known for its swimming pigs, adding an unexpected touch of character to its shores. Across the archipelago, low-lying islands and cays meet reefs, sandbars and brilliant shallows. Pale sand beneath clear water creates ribbons of turquoise, aquamarine and deep blue. From this height, land and sea seem to blur together, proving that sometimes the best view of paradise comes from above.

title: A field of poppies
caption: We will remember them
subtitle: Remembrance Day
description:
For Remembrance Day, we are looking out over a field of poppies, recognised as symbols of remembrance for more than a century.
Long known to flourish in the disturbed earth of battlefields, poppies were among the only plants to grow in the barren fields of northern France and Flanders in Belgium, after World War One. Their symbolism inspired the wartime poem In Flanders Fields, written by Canadian serviceman John McCrae in 1915. The poppy was later adopted by the Royal British Legion and artificial poppies made from silk were first sold in the UK in 1921, to raise money for ex-servicemen and the families of the fallen.
Our homepage today shows the Sun over a field of poppies, evoking the words of another World War One poem. The most famous lines of Laurence Binyon's poem, For the Fallen, are still used in remembrance services and on war memorials worldwide: "At the going down of the sun and in the morning, we will remember them."

title: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah, USA
caption: Architecture without an architect
subtitle: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah
description:
Just north of Moab, Utah, Arches National Park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches – the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.
North Window certainly has the look of a giant stone gateway, framing distant cliffs and ever-changing skies. But there was no blueprint, architect or construction crew involved. Instead, water, ice, temperature changes and gravity gradually wore away softer rock, leaving the tougher layers behind.

title: Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
caption: Hidden depths
subtitle: Ice on Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
description:
Dawn's first light reflects off the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by the peaks of the Rocky Mountains. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen methane bubbles, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the ice largely clear of snow, revealing the bubbles below throughout the winter. As spring arrives and the ice thaws, the trapped gas can escape into the atmosphere.
Despite its natural beauty, the lake is a human-made reservoir, created in 1972 when the Bighorn Dam was built on the North Saskatchewan River. Its icy winter landscapes and turquoise waters in summer make it a popular photography location throughout the year.

title: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
caption: The only way is up
description: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to more skyscrapers than any other city in the world. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters helped the island develop into a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth accelerated in the decades after the Second World War, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upwards, creating this distinctive skyline. As of 2026, Hong Kong has 569 completed buildings at least 150 metres tall — more than any other city in the world.
